title: Carnival in Galveston and in New Orleans
summary: Galveston's Carnival attempt, old neighbourhood masking, social clubs and dances during the season.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: Oh, yeah. What about Carnival? Did they have anything at all like Carnival?

There was something similar to what we do here, but not on a big scale in Galveston years ago. They had tried it. Well, there was a lot of Louisiana people that migrated into Galveston through Beaumont, Texas, and they tried to do the things there that was done in New Orleans, but the people in Texas wasn't ready for it.
Well, I always found Galveston is more like New Orleans than any other Texas town somewhere around.
In a way of the living, yeah. Well, that's because you had a migration there from Louisiana through Port Arthur and Beaumont.
There was something else that was going on here. I'll tell you about that. Well, what was Carnival like when you were growing up? Did we talk about that, about the different clubs and things?

Well, here in New Orleans? Here in New Orleans. I saw it when I was a barber. Yeah. Or something like that. Well, it always was a big day that we looked forward to. But as I've said before, it's changed so considerably from the old days. The old days, I imagine, there wasn't quite as many people as it is now because, man, this thing is mushroomed to an extent where you wonder where these people are going to actually go. And in the old days, there weren't so many, but a lot of masques. They had their own outfits and things like that, the music. And now it's commercialized. And in those days it was just a fun day. And you know what I'm talking about when I say commercialized.
Oh yeah. But you had little, what do you want to call them, clubs, bands?

Clubs and groups would get together. Yeah. What were some of the groups then? Well, neighborhood groups. They would mask like, imitate something in the storybook like a skeleton or a bear, something like this. A bunch of kids would get together in the neighborhood. And they'd go out in groups.
But they wouldn't have a name necessarily? Like a zulu?
Not necessarily. Well, no. You see, those are a few big organizations that had. You couldn't have, all these couldn't be clubs. It would have to just be a community thing.
Yeah. Well, I'm trying to think of some of the societies that are big.

Well, you had the Fros Amis for one. Yeah. But they didn't parade too much. Yeah. The Illinois club, was that downtown? That was downtown. That was the gentlemen's club. Mm-hmm. Oh, we used to play for that club. My big band. Illinois, I was a young man, 20. And well, you got quite a number of clubs like that, but not masking clubs. I see. But they would put on dances during the carnival season. Dances during the carnival season. Which they do yet. Yeah.
I wonder when the carnival season would start back then. Would you have any idea?
Same as it starts now. When it's- 12th, 9th, around. Right. Right. See, that's a tradition. Yeah. But now it's going back further and further. Well, that brings me back to the commercialism.

Yeah. Yeah. Well, that's why. In a way, it's a good thing, because it does keep- Some of these people could be- could stand to be kept on that toes. I mean, that thing looks so ratty, those floats and all that. Yeah. That's right. The commercial people sometimes do a better job than the people who are way up in society. What are some of the Texas holidays that you celebrate?
